nodes.text: GALEN'S BOOK ON THE PHASES IN DISEASES.

What the difference between ages is for living creatures, that is what they call 'phases' (*kairoi*) for diseases. For this term does not denote time simply, nor the appropriate time, in relation to which we also consider remedies; it denotes only the age of diseases, as has been said, which changes with the succession of times, just as the living creature changes with its ages. This seems to belong to all perishable bodies, to some more and to others less, since if their nature had remained always unaltered and unchanging, preserving its own substance, it would not perish. So just as we ourselves, once born, grow up to our prime, and then, beginning to waste from there, arrive at the final end, destruction, those of us who are going to pass through all the ages, in the same way each illness too, after the first establishment of its coming-to-be, takes the road of increase towards the greater and presses on to its peak, until, diminishing in proportion to its former growth, it comes to complete resolution. It might perhaps seem that the change of diseases over time differs from the age of living creatures only in this, that living creatures have a time of generation proper to them, in which all the parts necessary for life are formed, whereas diseases have no such proper time, but grow straight from their first onset. And this happens with good reason: for living creatures are bodies, while diseases are things that happen to bodies. The particular nature of bodies requires formation and generation, but the things that happen to them, since they need no formation, have their coming-to-be at once with their first onset and press on towards growth. For what coming-to-be could there be of an inflammation, like the formation of a creature in the womb? Or of erysipelas, or, as it may be, of a fever? For each of these appears, immediately on first beginning, to be of the same form as the greatest in the same kind, falling short of it only in size. At any rate the inflamed part becomes hotter than it was, with greater swelling, together with pain and tension; but these are small at the onset, and from then on grow up to a certain size, not the same in all cases, after which either the unnatural swelling is dispersed by remedies, with the pain and heat ceasing along with it, or it changes into pus. For these are the resolutions of an inflammation, if it is going to be resolved; let our discussion first be about these, the examination of diseases that are not resolved being postponed for the present to later. So there is no time proper, set apart and assigned to the coming-to-be of inflammation, distinct from that of growth, but the whole is one, the affection growing from the first onset up to the peak. So it is also with erysipelas and all the other [affections]. For fever too, I think, belongs in kind to unnatural heat; and no proper time of coming-to-be is marked off for this, but as soon as the body first begins to become hotter than it was with feverish heat, from then on one phase after another takes up the growth of the affection, up to the complete peak, which we understand in each thing to be its utmost magnitude.

This argument is plausible, and needs some noble contestant to answer it, who will show that the beginnings of diseases have a form of their own, as do living creatures being formed, and that the first time is assigned to this, bounded by its own limits. I would now be setting out to teach what I know on these matters, had not Archigenes' division, by some chance, come to mind as I reached this point in the argument; dividing diseases into the first and greatest phases, he places the peak straight after the beginning, leaving out the intermediate phase, the ascent. For where there seems to be no proper phase of the whole beginning, but from the first onset up to the peak all that lies between is increase, how could anyone grant Archigenes this, when he passes over what is agreed and readily posits what is disputed as though it were agreed? In this way he plainly betrays the argument utterly, though it needs a great contest to show that the beginning of the disease has a pattern of its own, differing not only in smallness from what follows it; but we shall now attempt to show that the beginning of the disease differs in a certain form from the ascent after it. The starting point of the argument will be a reminder drawn from what is plainly evident to all of us in many diseases. It was from this, I think, that almost all the physicians before Archigenes were moved to speak of a beginning of each disease, not that first onset alone, without extension, but assigning to it a certain length and breadth of time, sometimes considerable, and after it the ascent, then the peak, after which, of course, the so-called decline. At any rate we have seen some people, while doing any of the business of life, at first shiver slightly, then again and again feel a stronger irregularity and a more considerable shivering, so that they could neither do nor endure what they had earlier done without fault, but had to lie down and needed coverings; and some suffered this for three hours, some for fewer or more; and from then on they began to feel an unpleasant and unnatural heat, increasing little by little. For in these very cases the beginning of the paroxysm is plainly seen to differ in a distinctive form from the increase. It is clear that some call growth 'increase', just as certain others call it 'ascent'; we shall use all the terms as they occur to us, for they all denote one thing. This thing, then, which is called by three names, at some point stops and ceases from growth, and appears to remain equal to itself for some time, either longer or shorter; then from there it becomes less than itself, either quickly or over a longer time; and sometimes the condition of the feverish person appears in this way to return to freedom from fever, but sometimes it is overtaken by the onset of a second paroxysm having the same form as the one described before. And certainly sometimes the things described come upon the patient a second time, and often even a third, fourth and fifth, the disease going round in a kind of cycle from the same to the same through the same order. Physicians each call such a cycle a 'period'. Some of these are bounded within twenty-four hours, and they call them quotidian; some within forty-eight, that is, in two days and nights, which they call periods of tertian fevers; and others a time of seventy-two hours bounds, of which they call the fevers themselves quartan, and the whole cycle, which returns to the one beginning, a quartan period; so too a tertian period with a tertian fever, and the quotidian, returning each day, with quotidian fevers. But all periods sometimes arrive at freedom from fever, as in the fevers mentioned, quotidian, tertian and quartan; and sometimes only at a decline, coming either close to freedom from fever or further off.

For the sake of example, then, let our discussion first be about tertian fever. Such fevers begin with moderate shivering, then chilling of the extremities together with greater shivers, then they now have rigors and most of the body grows cold. Their pulse at this phase becomes harder and smaller than before, and clearly quicker in contraction, for those who know how to perceive contraction; whereas the dilatation is mostly slower than usual, especially at the onset, but sometimes it might seem to you to remain like its pre-existing state. Moreover, of the pauses, the one after contraction is somewhat longer; while the one after dilatation, in the same way as the latter, is mostly equal to what it was before, but sometimes not equal. These things naturally take place in some within two equinoctial hours, in others in either more or fewer; then the pulse, beginning to become larger and at the same time quicker and more frequent, adds little by little to each of the things mentioned. At once they also become hotter than they were, together with the said changes of the pulse, so that some feel much heat within while still chilled in the limbs, and, to put it all together, no small irregularity prevails in the body at this time. This is the second time after that first one, in which, from the previous state, the whole body grew cold and the pulse shifted to the opposite of what it was before. In the fever-free state, which let us call 'intermission', because Hippocrates too so named it, the pulse is in its natural state as far as our perception goes, and such is the best intermission; for it changes suddenly to the differences described a little earlier along with the creature's being chilled, and then turns back to the opposite with its being warmed. So the first time of the whole period is plainly the one in which the body grew cold with the said changes of the pulse, having arrived at this either from health or from an intermission; another, second, follows this, that of the change to the opposite of both pulse and heat, until the whole mass of the body becomes evenly hot; then after it a third, the heat still increasing, and the pulse advancing in proportion to it in size, speed and frequency; a fourth state is seen after the three mentioned, all the things mentioned keeping their magnitude equal to themselves, as far as our perception goes; then from there another, fifth, when the heat now becomes clearly less, vapour is excreted through the skin, and the pulse returns to its natural state, laying aside everything unnatural it had acquired in size, speed and frequency. In this time most of them also sweat, and after this comes the time of intermission, sixth after those mentioned. None of these is a hypothesis about something non-evident, but it plainly appears to happen thus almost daily in all who have tertian fever; and one must add to the argument what Hippocrates said, that up to this point even a non-physician could know correctly, if we remove the changes of the pulse from the account. For these are too subtle for the layman, but the change of heat, even if the sufferers did not wish to follow it, naturally goads and pricks them, so that it does not go unnoticed. At any rate all patients describe it thus: suddenly either an irregularity or a shivering ran through them, then from there, together with chilling of the extremities, the shivers intensified and rigor followed them; then again at some point the rigor stopped, the coldness of the extremities abated, and there was a sense of burning within, and thirst; after these again all irregularity went away, the whole body burned evenly, and this grew ever more so for them, and at some point the heat stood still and remained like itself; then later they felt it abating, and this did not stop happening until the state in which they first felt that they were no longer feverish. In tertian fevers, then, the particular differences of the period are of this kind; in others there are other differences of fevers, about which I shall speak next.

Now, first, let the account examine the one I set out first. The first phase, then, was the one adjoining the freedom from fever, which gives a sense of cold; we called it the beginning. The second is the one that lays aside the cold little by little, as has been said, and for the sake of brief teaching let it be called the phase of irregularity. Then after it a third, that of even increase. After this a fourth, that of standing still, and a fifth, that of diminution; then a sixth, that of freedom from fever. That the six standard differences stated exist in the periods of tertian fevers is a matter for perception and memory, not for logical demonstration. Since there are six of them, it is better to agree on names for them, for the sake of an indication that is both brief and clear. There is, as it were, a law common to all the Greeks: for things of which we have names given by the older writers, to use these; for those of which we have none, either to transfer [a name] from one of those we have, or to make [names] ourselves by some analogy with the things already named, or else to use by extension names established for other things. Anyone who wishes may neither keep to the usages customary among the Greeks nor, where he needs to make [names] himself, look to the aims stated; and this is common among the more recent physicians, since they were not educated in childhood in the education of children as the ancients were. We must therefore allow them to name things as they wish, since they are quarrelsome and shameless, and often indeed we must use names as they bid, in order to escape their chatter; for the patients will suffer no harm from lawlessness in names. But when they either steal some phase, passing over a whole one, or introduce into what has been said something that does not appear, they must not be permitted, since such an error now amounts to harm to the sick. In this matter, then, it is better first to have examined the causes of the errors by which most physicians go wrong, so that we ourselves may not err at all, and may show them too the true road to the matter, if they should wish. For some of them are so constituted that even if they had Apollo himself or Asclepius eager to teach them and urging them, they would never be able to listen and lend their ears, let alone receive in their soul what was said. But this will not be written for them. This, then, is the first and chief cause of their error: ignorance of the difference between diseases. For the tertian, as has just been said, usually moves and runs through what are, as it were, its ages, but not every disease has a similar movement. Therefore neither shall we rightly transfer to all [diseases] what we have said about tertians, nor will anyone else, starting from some other affection, rightly claim that one common account holds for all. This, then, is the first and greatest cause of their error.

The others I shall state next, in the order of their usefulness, once I have first given names to the stated phases of the tertian period. Now since Hippocrates said: 'Fevers that, not intermitting, become strong every third day are dangerous; but in whatever way they intermit, it signifies that they are without danger', one cannot take 'intermit' of any other part of the period, passing over the freedom from fever. For he certainly does not say 'in whatever way they decline', for that is not true. For the semitertian, though it is the worst of fevers, nonetheless reaches a decline clear to most people, and in all the others it is much the same in this respect, except for those called continuous (synochoi); for these alone of fevers have no perceptible decline, just as they have no whole period, nor any other of the differences mentioned before; but such a standing still at full magnitude for some time as we said belongs to tertians, that is what these have through almost their whole course. If, then, as I said, those that end in freedom from fever are without danger, at least by their own nature, as we showed in our discussions of them, Hippocrates called nothing else 'intermitting' than ending in freedom from fever. So one following the old usage might reasonably call the phase of freedom from fever in the periods of tertians an intermission; just as also [one might call] the standing still at the greatest magnitude, as perceived by us who touch [the patient] and by the patients themselves, the peak. So indeed the peak of the ages is the most complete, and Hippocrates is seen using this name too, as also 'to intermit'. Moreover the first part of the period, occurring on the first day upon the departure from the natural state, and on the third and fifth and the corresponding days, recurring in the same way after the intermission, is called the beginning not only by Hippocrates but by nearly all the other physicians too. After the beginning, plainly recognized by the cold, the second phase was that of irregularity, and the third that of increase, up to the peak. Not everyone has precisely observed that these, while sharing with one another, differ in form; and they name what is composed of both, as one whole, some 'increase', some 'growth', some 'ascent' of the paroxysm. And indeed they say something true; for after the first phase, in which the outer parts are chilled and the blood is plainly seen flowing together into the depth, there is another whole phase, standing in opposition to this whole one, the heat fighting against the cold and the blood stretching out towards the outer parts. And if they call it one in this way, as has just been said, it will make no difference to call this whole phase an ascent; but if, having called it so, they leave it undivided, they will do no small harm to the art. For the first phase in it, that of irregularity, indicates different remedies, not altogether the same as the phase after it, in which the state of the whole body is even, and there is an increase of what is present, which remains in the same form, up to the peak. The remaining one, the decline, is a single phase, like itself in form, except that its parts differ by more and less. But this holds also for the first phase, of the beginning, and for the second, of irregularity, and further for the third, of ascent. For each of these too has some difference, changing perceptibly part by part. For the beginning of each of the phases stated is not similar in all respects to its end, but they differ clearly from one another and from the middle phase. The beginning of the paroxysm, at any rate, has departed a little from the natural state, as the end has departed most; and where these have departed from one another by the greatest differences, there is surely some middle phase between them, further from the natural state than the beginning, but less far than the end. So too the beginning of the irregularity differs a little from the end of the first phase adjoining it, but departing further and being in the middle, it is somehow joined between the stated end of the first phase and the beginning of the third. By the same reasoning, I think, the parts of this second phase, of irregularity, that adjoin the beginnings of the third phase have a state close to those. So again the first parts of the third phase itself differ a little from the last parts of the second, while its last parts are somehow close to the form of the peak, and the middle of both stands equally apart from each extreme. So it is no wonder that, as with each of these phases, so with the decline there is a beginning, an end and a middle. And anyone who wished could call each of them by its own name. At any rate I hear physicians saying each time: 'The peak has just turned', 'now it is subsiding', 'now it is giving way', 'now it is remitting'. If, then, they say these things, it is not impossible for them to name the first parts of the decline a turning, or a subsiding, or a giving way, or a remission, or some of these, or all. And indeed one may also call the middle parts by one of the names stated, and the last parts in the same way; as Archigenes too names the last part of the decline remission. But he does badly in thinking it a different phase, differing in some form from the decline. Indeed, making of all the parts of the whole period a beginning, an end and a middle, he likewise makes the division of remission itself as though it were a phase of its own among those of the first division, which differ from one another in certain forms, not only by more and less. So he plainly errs in both respects, both removing from the first division the ascent, which all people grasp more clearly than the beginning, and adding remission at the end of the period. For if it reached freedom from fever, the difference of such a phase from all the others would be clear; but if the onset of the second paroxysm overtakes the decline, the decline being divided in three, then the [last] part of the whole decline may be called remission, but not thought to be another phase marked by some nature of its own, like those mentioned earlier. That all the parts of the tertian period can be seen separated from one another by clear differences is plain to anyone who has observed even one of the patients ill in this way; and if some of them are nameless, to the contentious we shall say 'first phase', and 'second', and 'third', and 'fourth', and 'fifth', then 'sixth', that of freedom from fever; but for those who know the use of names we shall ourselves agree on suitable ones. Let the first phase be given the proper name of beginning; the second that of irregularity; the third that of ascent; the fourth that of peak; the fifth that of decline; and let the sixth, that of freedom from fever, be called intermission.

The whole period can also be divided in another way, into larger parts, since it is possible to divide the whole of it into two: making one [part] that of the first paroxysm, from the first onset to the last remission, and the other that which lies between the decline and the onset of the second paroxysm. By the onset of a paroxysm I mean precisely the very first moment, which has no extent; this same [moment] they usually call the 'sign of attack' (*episēmasia*). And indeed what was said by Hippocrates, 'in the paroxysms one should hold back', I think was said according to this division. For having first said that it is proper, for those whose peak comes at once, to feed them lightly at once, and for those in whom it comes later, to feed them lightly towards that [point] and before it, but more richly before then, so that the sick man may hold out, he added: 'but in the paroxysms one must hold back', evidently teaching us to guard against only that phase which he calls the paroxysm. For we never feed in it, but we do in all the rest of the remission, at one time in one part of it and at another time in another. For sometimes [the remission] is simple, consisting only of decline, but sometimes it is made up of decline and intermission. This, then, is the division of the single period into two parts, we calling the one part of it, the earlier, the paroxysm, and the second, which follows it, either remission, as just now, or, as some do, intermission. For not a few physicians call everything after the peak an intermission, whatever its nature, whether it ends in freedom from fever or not. But let us keep the names stated before, so that no unclarity arises in the account, and let everything after the paroxysm be called remission, though we do not object, as I said, if someone wishes to call the whole of it intermission, or decline, or giving way, or subsiding, or abatement. For our purpose is not to quarrel about names, but to examine the parts of the period: how many they are in number and in what way they differ from one another.

This, then, is the division of all fevers that end in freedom from fever, quotidian, tertian and quartan, as having six parts which differ from one another in well-marked forms; another is that of those which do not intermit, which are divided into five parts. These too are very numerous, some having paroxysms every day, some every third day; those every fourth day, however, are not often seen to occur, but rarely, for most of their kind cease in freedom from fever. Of these too, the quotidian, tertian and quartan fevers that do not cease in freedom from fever, the form is twofold. For some of them lay aside the size of the pulse and its speed and its frequency and its hardness; but some bring the other three back to the natural state, but keep the speed, some more, some less. But it is not for the present account to make distinctions about those; for our purpose is to enumerate the parts of the period in each kind of disease. Having said, then, a little earlier, that there are six [parts] in all in the intermittent fevers, we next go through the parts of the non-intermittent ones, saying that they are five, when the others are present in them in a similar way and only that of freedom from fever is lacking. The similarity in the other parts is of necessity this: that the onset of the paroxysms occurs with contraction (I call by this name the onset with chilling, for upon this it follows that the pulses move more inwards, with smallness, as the blood withdraws into the viscera), upon which in turn of necessity follows the [phase] of irregularity, and then next that of ascent, of peak and of decline. In those cases, however, in which the onset of the paroxysm occurs without perceptible contraction, the three phases must fall together into one, and the whole up to the peak becomes ascent. For where there was no contraction, plainly there was no irregularity either. But I have never seen the peak missing; rather, in all fevers a perceptible evenness always persists for some time. The onset, however, I have seen countless times without the symptoms of the beginning that have been mentioned, of which the most important was the chilling that accompanies almost all beginnings of paroxysms, as also the inward movement of the arteries, about which more has been said in the treatise on the pulses; in the present account it suffices to define it by the speed of the contraction. As for the other symptoms and signs that are proper to the beginning of the paroxysms, it was said earlier that some follow the chilling, while others arise in other ways: smallness of the pulses, infrequency and slowness of the dilatation follow the chilling, but rigor [arises] from other causes, which we described in [the work on] the causes of symptoms. But this whole class [of signs] of the paroxysms is entirely lost, as I said, and we have often stopped many who had either been sent to the bath or been told to take food by these wonderful physicians, as though they had already passed the suspected hours of the paroxysm. It happens that these [physicians], not knowing how to feel the artery precisely, fall into such errors. For in all who have paroxysms in this way the contraction becomes faster; but recognising it is not for everyone, but this task, if any in the art, especially requires sufficient practice, which cannot be undertaken before one has been trained in the method described by us in the first [book] of On the Diagnosis of Pulses. If, then, someone is able to recognise the contraction of the arteries, he may set down as the beginning of the period that very part of the paroxysm in which he recognised that the contraction had become quicker without the dilatation, and what comes after it as ascent, up to the peak. But if he cannot recognise even this, and the onset appears to him to have occurred wholly without oppression, he will call the whole part of the paroxysm up to the peak ascent, or increase, or growth, dividing it into first, last and middle [parts] by more and less, not by different forms, as I was saying earlier in the case of perceptible chillings. In such fevers, then, there will be three phases in all: growth, peak, diminution; for it is no worse to call diminution that phase in which something is taken away from the size of the fever. But in those in which there is no period, as in the so-called continuous (synochos) fevers, in these fevers there is no paroxysm at all, nor the parts mentioned before; yet the parts of the whole disease, at different times, exist in these too, recognised in other ways than the phases in the paroxysms. These I shall describe a little later, especially since all physicians go wrong about them, even though Hippocrates taught most correctly about them.

But now let us return in our account to those which have paroxysms in some period, distinguishing whatever has remained unexamined in them. One thing first of all I bid you remember: that all our account from the beginning up to here has been about simple periods. For in interwoven ones the phase after the peak is sometimes narrowed, the sign of attack of another paroxysm breaking in early, before the earlier period has been precisely completed; and often the fever by its own nature is of the intermittent kind, like the tertian, but the interweaving leaves no time of freedom from fever to the earlier period, the second paroxysm having broken in before the first was resolved. I have spoken about such interweavings in two treatises, On Crises and On the Differences of Fevers, where mixture is also distinguished from interweaving. The semitertian, at any rate, was shown to arise from the mixture and blending of a quotidian and a tertian fever. And often one of the simple fevers, either a tertian or a quotidian, is interwoven with the semitertian itself; but such complexity does not belong to the present treatise, for here it suffices to articulate precisely the phases proper to each of the fevers; for in this way above all we would be able readily to distinguish what is interwoven among them. The precisely simple ones, then, have been described; next I shall speak of the mixed ones. Sometimes, then, there occurs a shivering onset, having all the distinguishing marks proper to the beginning except rigor, and sometimes even the appearance of this; for violent shivering would seem to be either a beginning of rigor or a small rigor, but genuine rigor, such as there is in tertian and quartan fevers, such [a fever] does not take on, and for this reason I call it shivering; and much more because, having shown some signs of the second phase, it again produces a shivering beginning of another onset, which some call recurrence (*epanalēpsis*), others redoubling (*epanadiplōsis*); and sometimes it does this a second time, and in some patients at times even a third, and then only with difficulty later unfolds evenly, ascending to the peak. This fever never ceases in freedom from fever. For the time it takes to reach the peak is very long, and the decline is without perceptible transpiration; and it falls much further short of passing into freedom from fever with sweat. Just as, then, the paroxysm from the first onset arrives at the peak over a long time, in the same way it diminishes little by little from the peak. And so on the following day another paroxysm comes upon them, likewise shivering, but not having recurrences in the same way as the previous one, or if it should ever rarely have them, it would make only one, brief and small. This paroxysm too ascends to the peak over a long time, and likewise declines over no short time, and for this very reason on the third day the same paroxysm as on the first follows, and then again on the fourth the same as on the second, and so on continually in succession. Wishing to address this fever by a single name for the sake of concise and clear teaching, I have given it the name semitertian. If, then, Hippocrates too called such a fever semitertian, as I am persuaded, you would gain two things from the account: that you learn a medical fact, and that you apply an ancient name to it; but if someone thinks that some other fever is called semitertian by Hippocrates, and considers me mistaken in the naming, let him learn the thing itself. For that such a fever as I have described does occur, the account here no longer needs the witness either of Hippocrates or of anyone else, since we see it almost every day, and especially in Rome. For just as different [evils abound] in different places, so in this city this evil abounds. Next to it lies another, which neither brings another paroxysm on the second day nor recurrences on the first and third. Nor is the manner of this one single: for sometimes it makes its onset without shivering, sometimes with shivering, and sometimes also with clear chilling of the extremities; and this fever has sometimes been seen, even without perceptible chilling, to have the five phases: beginning, irregularity, increase, peak and decline. As to the times, now distinguished: its beginning is brief, and its irregularity is brief too; but the [times] of the ascent are not alike in all, but in some (not) brief, in others of longer time; and indeed the phase of the peak is in every case of perceptible and extended time, but differs not a little by more and less. So too the [times] of the decline are long in all, but differ in that in some [the fever] perceptibly abates and gives hope of ceasing quickly, and after this it stands still, keeping the remaining size of the decline equal; but in others it makes the whole decline slow from beginning to end, so that even if you touch [the pulse] at longer intervals of time, it will seem to you to have abated something, certainly, but this very little. Such are some, and there are other particular differences, of the fevers that have paroxysms every third day, all of which I call tertian-like (*tritaiophyeis*); they are most useful for knowledge of the condition from which they are kindled, but useless for the present treatise. For our purpose here is to define both the phases in the periods and those of the whole disease, for the sake of the timely use of remedies, which such complexity does not help at all, just as neither does that of the [fevers] varied in the quotidian pattern; for of these too not a few, having paroxysms every day, have no intermission. Nevertheless I shall describe a few of their differences by way of example, not as useful for the present subject, but because some physicians are entirely puffed up by the things they babble irrationally, and win a reputation among the unintelligent as diligent and hard-working and knowing something wiser than those who write only what is useful.

The paroxysm, then, of fevers that have paroxysms every day sometimes begins without a clear chilling, and sometimes with one; and the features proper to the beginning persist in some for a longer time, in others for a shorter; and likewise also those of the irregularity, in some for a longer time, in others for a shorter. And after this the fever ascends to the peak in a longer time than those that have paroxysms every third day. It also has a feature of this kind, which occurs in those too, though rarely, but appears much more in this one: having made a clear ascent, it halts for some time, adding nothing, and then adds again. So also in the decline it either makes the abatement evenly, or halts in between at the same size, in some for one hour, in others for two, and after this abates. And indeed, up to the onset of the second paroxysm, in some it abates, while in others it remains at whatever size it is. But this belongs rather to the [fevers] with paroxysms every third day, because their period is also longer. For the period of fevers that have paroxysms every third day is roughly double in time, if it is compared with that of the daily ones. So for this reason the remnant of the decline itself plainly lasts a long time, remaining at an equal size. There are many other modes of periods too, varied by particular differences, which are superfluous for the present matters. I have mentioned some of them for this reason: that those physicians who do not recognise that such teaching does not belong to the present inquiry have written about them, going wrong even in their account of them. But now is not the time to refute them in an inquiry not proper to it; you will learn scientifically that they babble useless things, and that, although Hippocrates admirably discovered the method concerning them, no one has worked it out, and besides this most have corrupted it, especially in that part of the account where I am going to connect the remedies to the phases described. I shall do this after I have shown the phases of the whole disease; for up to this point I have gone through only those of the part.
